<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 25 Oct 2026 05:40:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Shares slump slightly as prospects for peace in Middle East seem further away]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/08/11/shares-slump-slightly-as-prospects-for-peace-in-middle-east-seem-further-away/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/08/11/shares-slump-slightly-as-prospects-for-peace-in-middle-east-seem-further-away/Tue, 11 Aug 2026 18:11:13 +0000Global stocks held their nerve on Tuesday, as investors on either side of the Atlantic reacted with differing degrees of confidence that a peace deal will be agreed between the US and Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Closer to home, shares dipped slightly during an otherwise light trading day.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell by 0.32 per cent on Tuesday to close the trading day at 14,233.55, following another light volume session of trading in Ireland.

The banking sector saw mixed results, with AIB’s share price falling by 0.92 per cent to close at €10.76 and PTSB remaining steady on €2.95. Bank of Ireland fared better than its rivals, edging up 0.24 per cent, to end the day at €18.97.

Housebuilder Glenveagh Properties saw its share price rise by 1.62 per cent to close at €2.51, while insulation and building material specialists Kingspan Group was up 1.99 per cent on €97.15 in advance of a €900 million deal that was announced after markets closed.

Stock in wind and solar energy group Greencoat Renewables was up 2.35 per cent, the largest percentage rise of any index constituent.

Glanbia saw its share price fall back 2.41 per cent to close the day at €23.44, while stock in Ryanair also slid, by 0.88 per cent to €24.68.

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange remained largely steady throughout the day. While the blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell by 0.17 per cent, it was somewhat offset by the mid-cap FTSE 250 gaining by 0.22 per cent at close of business.

In a similar day to its Irish neighbours, the UK banking sector saw prices come under pressure. Shares in Lloyds Banking Group on the FTSE 100 fell by 0.74 per cent by close, while NatWest dropped by 0.34 per cent.

Oil and gas giant BP saw much more positive returns, with its shares adding 2.15 per cent despite concerns growing that a peace-deal between the US and Iran, which could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, is looking less likely.

Vodafone Group rebounded by 1.28, having fallen by 3.07 per cent the previous trading day. On the more domestically-focused FTSE 250, shoe makers Doc Marten’s share price rose by 3.34 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, stocks remained steady around the record highs they have hovered close to in recent trading days. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose fractionally, by 0.01 per cent, as investors balanced economic optimism closer to home with geopolitical risks further afield.

With Bloomberg News reporting comments from Pakistan’s defence minister that the US and Iran are nearing “some sort of agreement”, oil prices broadly increased by 1.2 per cent on Tuesday. The energy sector jumped 1.7 per cent, while tech shares rose 1.1 per cent, providing further support. That sector remains among Europe’s top performers this year, up about 24 per cent year to date.

Danish facility manager, ISS gained 4.4 per cent after reporting half-year results above estimates. Spirax Group slid 5.6 per cent to the bottom of the Stoxx 600 after the engineering firm ​reiterated its full-year forecast for mid-single-digit organic revenue growth and margin expansion.

NEW YORK

Early trading of stocks on Wall Street indicated that US investors were matching the caution of their European counterparts, largely avoiding heavy bets on the market.

Both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell slightly by 1pm New York time, by 0.16 per cent and 0.18 per cent respectively.

The strongest stocks on the S&P during early trade appeared to be investment firm KKR, rising by around 6 per cent, and Axon Enterprise, also around 6 per cent.

Engineering firm Amentum Holdings was in the red from early, with its share price falling some 6 per cent.

Household brand names Apple, Nike and Amazon were off to rocky starts on the Dow Jones Industrial Average Tuesday morning, with the tech giant falling some half a per cent, the sports brand by around 2.6 per cent and the online retail giant by 2.3 per cent. – Additional reporting: Reuters, Bloomberg

]]>Spencer Platt<![CDATA[Mortgage interest rates up slightly but dip below euro zone average]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/08/12/mortgage-interest-rates-up-slightly-but-dip-below-euro-zone-average/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/08/12/mortgage-interest-rates-up-slightly-but-dip-below-euro-zone-average/Wed, 12 Aug 2026 12:39:48 +0000Irish mortgage rates fell below the euro zone average for the first time in over three years in June despite a slight rise in the interest charged on new loans.

The average interest rate on new mortgage agreements at the end of June was 3.49 per cent, according to new Central Bank figures. That is one basis point (0.01 of a percentage point) higher than in May but 11 basis points lower than the same time last year.

That compares with the 0.14 per cent average being offered by the banks for overnight deposits, or 1.86 per cent on fixed term savings.

The average rate of interest on mortgage loans across the euro zone rose faster in the month, to 3.51 per cent, marking the first time the Irish result was lower than the pan-European average since February 2023.

The Irish rate was the 12th highest across the euro bloc in June, according to the Central Bank, falling between the 3.5 per cent average in Italy and the 3.27 per cent in France. Ireland’s position is unchanged from the previous month and down five places from the same time last year.

“Today’s figures confirm what a lot of mortgage holders have been bracing for,” said Sorcha Timoney, mortgage team manager at advisory firm NFP Ireland. “Anyone coming off a fixed rate or on a variable will feel this increase in their monthly repayments.

“Due to strong competition in the Irish market, the gap between what Irish borrowers pay and the wider euro area average has been narrowing but if rates continue to creep up, we could see this gap widening once again,” she said.

The Central Bank data show that fixed rate mortgages accounted for 93 per cent of the volume of all new home loan agreements in June, an increase of eight percentage points from the same period last year. Fixed rate loan interest averaged 3.46 per cent, two basis points higher than in May.

New variable rate mortgages had a weighted average interest rate of 3.96 per cent last month, “the lowest level since December 2022”, the Central Bank said and down seven basis points from May and 12 basis points in annual terms.

Lenders sanctioned €1.1 billion in new mortgage loans in June, up 13 per cent on the May number and the highest figure so far this year. The figure is 8.5 per cent ahead of the €996 million in new loans agreed in the same month last year.

The volume of renegotiated mortgages totalled €586 million last month, €301 million higher than June 2025’s figure and 94 per cent of which had fixed interest rates. People renegotiating their loans did better on interest rates, agreeing an average rate of 3.23 per cent, down two basis points from May and close to a quarter percentage point from this time last year.

Analysts and advisers were quick to point to a number of potential factors for the increase in Irish mortgage interest rates, from competition in the domestic market to ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Trevor Grant, chairman of Irish Mortgage Advisors, said borrowers should not be “unduly alarmed by the widely anticipated September ECB rate hike”, adding that competition was the main factor influencing home loan rates in Ireland.

“Most lenders did not move on the back of the ECB rise in June, though they may see any ECB increase in September as an opportunity to increase rates,” he said.

Rachel McGovern, chief executive of Brokers Ireland, advised people to examine their options.

“Regardless of where you are in the cycle of your loan, now is the time to review because when things turn changes could happen more rapidly than you expect, that is the nature off such changes,” she said, adding that “already we’re seeing niche lenders increasing rates”.

However, as Bonkers.ie spokesman Daragh Cassidy, noted, Ireland’s three big lenders – AIB, Bank of Ireland and PTSB – which account for around 90 per cent of all new mortgage lending in Ireland, have yet to increase their rates.

An analysis by Bonkers.ie found that for an average first-time buyer borrowing €300,000 with a 10 per cent deposit, variable mortgage rates currently range from 3.85 per cent to 4.85 per cent. Rates for a three-year fixed mortgage range from 3.2 per cent to 5.45 per cent, it said.

Away from mortgages, lenders did raise interest rates on other consumer loans more dramatically – by 23 basis points – to 7.48 per cent. The average for variable rates loans – which accounts for over three-quarters of all consumer borrowing – was 8.09 per cent that month, compared to 5.43 per cent for fixed rate loans.

There was €266 million of new consumer borrowing agreed in the month.

On fixed term savings, the 1.86 per cent average available in Ireland is the 13th best rate available across the euro zone, comfortably ahead of the 1.21 per cent in Greece but still well shy of rates above 2.5 per cent available in Finland and the Netherlands.

The Central Bank said Irish savers put €1.6 billion into fixed term deposits in June. That was 14 per cent up on May and 43 per cent stronger than in June 2025.

]]>Andy Rain<![CDATA[Freeze minimum wage until 2030, urges business advisory group]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/14/set-up-350m-ai-training-scheme-and-freeze-minimum-wage-says-business-advisory-group/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/14/set-up-350m-ai-training-scheme-and-freeze-minimum-wage-says-business-advisory-group/Thu, 13 Aug 2026 23:01:00 +0000A €5 billion investment fund, a €350 million artificial intelligence (AI) training programme and no increase in minimum wage until 2030 form part of “a pro-growth agenda” that the Government should adopt to support SMEs, according to a prebudget submission by Azets Ireland.

The professional services firm said that by adopting these measures, and more, the Government would move from “crisis management to strategic investment” for “the next phase of Ireland’s economic success”.

Azets Ireland said small businesses were “the backbone of the domestic economy and employ two in every three workers in local communities across the country” yet were “disproportionately impacted by rising costs and economic uncertainty”.

The advisory company, which employs about 350 people here, called on the Government “to postpone any planned increases in excise duty until greater stability returns to energy markets”, warning that “rising fuel costs could further squeeze already tight margins” for small businesses.

To alleviate these pressures and promote growth in the sector, Azets proposes the creation of a “home-grown investment fund” of €5 billion from “excess corporation tax from multinationals” to be allocated for “strategic investment in small and mid-sized businesses” indigenous to Ireland.

“This fund would help to rebalance the domestic economy and support more firms to grow and compete globally,” the firm said.

It also advocates for “€350 million in funding to be ring-fenced from the National Training Fund for AI skilling and training for SMEs to enable them to upskill their people and enhance future competitiveness”.

“If SMEs are to fully harness the potential of AI, they need greater support to develop the right skills for the future,” Azets Ireland’s chief executive Neil Hughes said.

This “would help businesses build these crucial capabilities and directly enhance future competitiveness”.

It called for “a roadmap to reduce capital gains tax to 20 per cent by 2030, in line with standard rates across Europe”. The standard rate currently applied is 33 per cent.

The firm also advocated for “a simplified route for mid-sized firms to avail of the R&D tax credit”. Hughes said these measures “would help unlock access to much needed capital that can support these businesses accelerate innovation and growth”.

“Amid the escalating cost of doing business, the firm is calling for deferring planned increases in employer PRSI rates to 2027 and a cap on future contribution rates for SMEs,” the company said.

“Azets is also calling for freezing the minimum wage rate until 2030 and additional statutory entitlements for employees to help small and family-owned businesses grappling with rising labour costs.”

Hughes said “with the right supports in place, indigenous businesses can drive the next phase of Irish economic growth, creating jobs, strengthening communities and building a more resilient economy for the future”.

The budget is due to be announced on October 6th by the Minister for Finance Simon Harris and the Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers.

]]>Leah Farrell<![CDATA[Global stocks retreat from record highs amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/13/global-stocks-retreat-from-record-highs-amid-geopolitical-and-economic-uncertainty/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/13/global-stocks-retreat-from-record-highs-amid-geopolitical-and-economic-uncertainty/Thu, 13 Aug 2026 18:00:00 +0000While better-than-expected consumer data in the US boosted investors’ confidence in the market during early trading hours on Wall Street, poor returns for UK-listed mining companies sparked a two-week low on the London Stock Exchange.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell 0.47 per cent on Thursday to close at 14,385.15, following falls in share prices from Ryanair and Great Western Mining.

Building materials group Kingspan saw its share price fall 0.87 per cent on Thursday to close at €102.90.

This comes on the day it announced its acquisition of a majority stake in Grupo Ltd, an Argentinian structural insulated panels manufacturer, and two days after the Cavan-based insulation giant signalled an expansion into its data centre presence with the purchase of BMC Manufacturing Group.

Ryanair’s stock dropped a clean 1 per cent to close on €24.65, while the Nevada-based, Dublin-listed Great Western Mining saw its shares decrease 9.5 per cent, to close on a share price of 3.8 cent.

Kerry Group had a more positive result, with its share price increasing 1.5 per cent to close at €83.90. Glanbia rose 1.20 per cent to €23.64, while Origin Enterprises followed slightly behind, rising 1.01 per cent to close at €4.50.

The banking sector saw mixed returns, with AIB gaining 0.6 per cent to close at €10.69, although Bank of Ireland dropped 0.2 per cent to close at €18.875. Permanent TSB saw no change in its share price, holding at €2.95.

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange was rattled as the blue-chip FTSE 100 index was reduced to a two-week low, a result hardly offset by the more domestically-minded FTSE 250’s increase of 0.1 per cent.

The FTSE 100 fell 0.56 per cent at close after the UK-based Chilean mining company Antofagasta’s downbeat copper production ​forecast sparked losses in the mining sector and offset any relief from stronger-than-expected economic growth in June.

The company’s share fell by 6.8 per cent after it ceased operations at a primary mine. This sparked losses among other mining companies too, with Rio Tinto and Anglo American dropping 4.8 per cent and 3.5 per cent respectively.

Property developer Berkeley saw greater returns, increasing its share price by 2.76 per cent, as did Lion Finance by 5.19 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, shares dipped slightly and retreated further from the record highs they reached for days in a row last week, as continental investors grow more cautious about where their money goes.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index decreased fractionally by 0.04 per cent on Thursday despite impressive gains by some. Dutch payment company Adyen jumped 16.40 at the close of business after it shared financial results from the first half of the year and raised its outlook for the second half.

British companies trading on the euro stock market saw minimal change in their share prices: Lloyds Banking was up 0.09 per cent, oil giant BP was down 1.56 per cent, while Barclays bank decreased 0.08 per cent.

NEW YORK

During early trading hours on Wall Street, US investors felt renewed confidence in the financial markets after better-than-expected producer price data further reduced expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase rates next month.

Both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 rose before midday New York time, by about 0.2 per cent and 0.7 per cent respectively.

Tech stocks swelled to an intraday record high on the S&P 500 while oil suppliers took a slight hit, with higher inventories and lower global demand forecasts offsetting widespread geopolitical concerns.

Prospects of a US-Iran peace deal were bogged down with renewed pessimism as Washington and Tehran traded accusations that the other party is not prepared to agree to a deal. – Additional reporting: Reuters.

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[NTMA increases State savings rates for first time in three years ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/ireland-state-saving-rates-increased-for-first-time-in-three-years/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/ireland-state-saving-rates-increased-for-first-time-in-three-years/Mon, 17 Aug 2026 11:27:07 +0000Ireland’s State savings will see an increase in the rates applied to newly-issued products from the end of the month, after the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) announced its first hike since October 2023.

From August 30th, the variable rate used to calculate the monthly prize bond fund will increase from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent, meaning “the weekly draw will have more prizes and higher-value prizes,” the NTMA said.

While the monthly top prize of €500,000 will remain unchanged, the weekly top prize will double to €100,000.

Other changes to the fund include 50 prizes of €1,000 being awarded every week, instead of the current arrangement of 20 prizes of €1,000 and 20 of €500. The remaining weekly prizes will increase from €75 to €100.

Some 10,000 prizes are expected to be awarded every week. All prizes are tax free.

The variable rate applied to post-office savings bank deposit accounts will rise by 0.5 per cent to 1.25 per cent, with deposit interest retention tax applied.

The annual equivalent rates (AER) will increase for three-year saving bonds by 0.64 per cent to 1.96 per cent; five-year saving certificate rates by 0.55 per cent to 2.29 per cent; six-year instalment saving rates by 0.58 per cent to 2.33 per cent; and 10-year national solidarity bond rates by 0.65 per cent to 2.66 per cent.

Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the move was “a measure that will help people who are saving and investing”.

The various State savings products form part of Ireland’s national debt. The total value of State savings holdings was €23.9 billion at the end June 2026.

The NTMA’s director of funding and debt management, Dave McEvoy, said “retail savings were an important element of the NTMA’s funding strategy, providing diversification in our funding an investor base”.

“In setting rates on Ireland State savings, the NTMA seeks a balance between providing customers with a safe and competitive savings option and providing long-term value to the exchequer,” he said.

]]>Sam boal/Collins Photos<![CDATA[Harvey Nichols Dundrum will not accept gift cards bought before liquidators’ appointment]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/harvey-nichols-dundrum-will-not-accept-gift-cards-bought-before-liquidators-appointment/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/harvey-nichols-dundrum-will-not-accept-gift-cards-bought-before-liquidators-appointment/Mon, 17 Aug 2026 17:15:53 +0000The provisional liquidators of the Irish company behind the Harvey Nichols store in Dundrum have said they are not currently able to redeem gift cards or fulfil online sales issued by the retailer before they were appointed on August 13th.

John Boland and Nicholas O’Dwyer of Grant Thornton were appointed as joint provisional liquidators last week after the High Court heard the Irish business was insolvent with net liabilities of €28.2 million by the end of the 2026 financial year.

This followed the sale of its UK parent to Mike Ashley’s Frasers group through what is known as a prepack administration process in the UK.

Frasers supplied support for the Dundrum store to reopen on Saturday and to continue trading for now, while the liquidators seek to sell the business.

However, in a notice posted on the Irish store’s website, Harvey Nichols said it was “currently unavailable online” and that any “orders placed and gift cards purchased prior to August 13th, 2026, fall under the ownership structure preceding this transition”.

“Refunds relating to these orders cannot be processed by Harvey Nichols directly; customers with an outstanding refund from this period are asked to contact, HNCustomers@fticonsulting.com.”

In a statement to The Irish Times in relation to gift cards and online orders, the liquidators said they had “entered into an arrangement” that enabled the Dundrum store to open again for trading from August 15th.

“The arrangement allows the business to continue trading and receive stock while the JPLs [joint provisional liquidators] assess the options available to the company,” they added.

Harvey Nichols Dundrum was kept on life support for 20 years. But could it still have a future?

“Continued trading helps preserve value in the business, maintain employment and provides an opportunity to determine whether a sale or other transaction can be achieved in the interests of the company stakeholders. At this time, there can be no certainty as to the outcome of that process.

Traditional early career progression has largely been uprooted in recent years as recruitment efforts have reduced, in part due to the broader tightening of the economy, but also as a result of the rapid development in artificial intelligence (AI) resulting in fewer workers needed to undertake certain tasks.

Employment data from the Central Statistics Office (CSO) demonstrates the difficulty many young people experience in securing work and, perhaps, confirms the fears of parents across the country.

Every month so far this year, the youth unemployment rate in the State has been at least double the unemployment rate for those aged over 25 – and in January, July and August it was more than three times higher than the general population.

But raw employment data does not tell the full story behind the tightening of recruitment inside Ireland’s leading companies. Figures from Chartered Accountants Ireland, the professional body, show how the traditional training contract has become a less viable option.

While its total student intake increased by 11 per cent from 2023 to 2024, this was in large part due to a higher uptake of its “flexible route”, which enables people to earn an accountancy qualification without a training contract from an accountancy firm, jumping from 10 per cent of candidates in 2023 to 16 per cent in 2024.

“We were actually just discussing this at lunchtime,” Curran says, mentioning the other interns she has worked alongside this summer.

“And don’t be afraid to ask questions – you’re expected to be curious. But, what I would say is ask a question once, take note of it, remember it, try not to ask the same question over and over again. If you make a mistake, learn from it, grow from it [and] try not to make the same mistake again.”

The committee keeps an eye out for a number of qualities – “we’re more focused on green flags than red flags, for want of a better word”, O’Shaughnessy says. – but an all-encompassing one is the ability to work well on a team.

“We need to be able to work closely and collaboratively with both our clients and our colleagues. Marian Finnegan

After 29 years, while managing director of the residential arm of the company, Finnegan said “it felt like the natural next step” to head the business.

Kenny Jacobs

In February of this year, the High Court heard Kenny Jacobs would “voluntarily step down” as chief executive of the DAA, which operates Dublin and Cork airports, after an out-of-court settlement closed the lawsuit brought against the semi-State body.

Suspended from his position just before Christmas following a months-long rift with DAA colleagues, Jacobs had previously agreed an exit package with its board, however Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien refused to sign off on it.

Following an ugly court case – what is seen as the fieriest feud to engulf the airport operator in decades – Jacobs ultimately left with a parting sum in the region of €480,000.

Garry Moroney

Marking a departure from the managing director title bestowed on previous commercial leaders of The Irish Times Group, tech-exec-turned-media-mogul Garry Moroney was appointed its first chief executive in November 2025.

Previously chief executive of travel management platform Roomex, Moroney had founded two companies before this and worked at McKinsey at the start of his career.

Alongside this newspaper, the group owns the Irish Examiner and Echo, a range of regional newspapers and websites MyHome.ie and RIP.ie. In early August, it announced its intention to wind down breakingnews.ie.

Deirdre Veldon, the former deputy editor of The Irish Times, stepped down as the group’s managing director in September 2025 having served in the position since late 2022.

Andrew Yaxley

UK-based Tesco Group reshuffled its Irish operations in August, with former Tesco Ireland chief executive Andrew Yaxley returning to lead the all-island business here after eight years in Britain.

He effectively traded roles with Geoff Byrne, who will take over as chief executive of the wholesaler Booker Group in September. Both men will continue to sit on the group’s executive committee.

Caroline Bocquel

Moving from the top job at Ireland’s Seafood Development Agency (Bord Iascaigh Mhara) to the top job at the State’s national tourism development authority, Caroline Bocquel was appointed chief executive of Fáilte Ireland in November last year.

Fáilte Ireland’s previous chief executive, Paul Kelly, left the tourism authority in March after eight years in the post. He now serves as chief executive of the Royal Dublin Society (RDS).

Albert Manifold

Eoin Tonge

Primark returned to its Irish leadership roots with the appointment of Eoin Tonge as its chief executive in March this year, 17 years after its founder Arthur Ryan left the position.

Between the two, from 2009 to 2025, the role was held by British-born Paul Marchant, who resigned in March last year following an investigation into alleged inappropriate behaviour towards a female colleague.

He says the Irish firm has spent a “significant amount of money” on training and upskilling its staff so it can deliver for clients.

This all feeds into a plan to achieve turnover of €1.3 billion by 2031, whichwould represent growth of about €400 million over the period.

O’Keeffe estimates that EY is the largest Big Four firm in the market, some 40 per cent bigger than KPMG, in second place.

Which brings us to the impact of artificial intelligence on EY’s business, specifically the potential impact on its graduate programme and overall headcount.

Frank O’Keeffe

It is also using Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude on a day-to-day basis. “We have nearly one and a half thousand technology consultants that you could tag to being AI ... but everybody else is using AI tools and processes and licenses to make sure that we do the most effective roles to support our clients. Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan?

Can it save you money?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/23/every-lidl-helps-when-it-comes-to-saving-money-on-your-mobile-phone-costs/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/23/every-lidl-helps-when-it-comes-to-saving-money-on-your-mobile-phone-costs/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:44:11 +0000Earlier this month Lidl created quite a stir when it announced it had started selling something somewhat unexpected – and not just the jack hammers, blow torches and inflatable swimming pools that we have grown accustomed to finding in the middle aisles.

The new unexpected thing that Lidl started selling was mobile phones – or at least access to the Irish mobile phone network.

The top line was quite alluring.

The first 100,000 people who signed up to Lidl Connect were promised a monthly charge of €8.99 for life. They were given the option of picking up a physical SIM in any Lidl store for an additional €0.99 or selecting an eSIM and completing their registration via the Lidl Plus app at no extra cost.

The monthly rolling plans require no long-term commitment and include unlimited 5G data; unlimited calls and texts to any Irish and UK network; 50GB of EU and UK roaming data and 100 international minutes per month to more than 38 countries.

People who decided to migrate to Lidl Connect were told they could keep their existing mobile numbers or choose a new one if they were so inclined.

But bells and whistles and portability aside, it was the price tag that got Lidl the most attention, although we should point out that its offering is not all that much cheaper than Tesco’s SIM-only deal, which costs a tenner a month.

Lidl Connect is, however, much cheaper than what many Irish mobile phone users who are on long-term contracts are accustomed to paying.

How much cheaper?

That is the interesting thing.

A typical bill pay customer might be paying €50 a month – a price that might include a free handset every couple of years. Or might not.

Leaving aside the handset for a moment, a 20-year-old who chooses the €8.99 a month deal at Lidl and lives for the next 70 years and never leaves the German discounter will end up paying a total of €7,551.60 over the course of their – hopefully – long and happy life.

Were this notional 20-year-old to instead sign up to a monthly bill pay deal with one of the State’s leading operators and live for the same 70 years without ever switching, the total cost of their mobile phone will come in at €42,000 in today’s money.

Now we know we are making a lot of assumptions here, not least that we will still be using money, mobile phones or indeed Lidl 70 years from now.

But you get the idea. SIM-only, pay-as-you-go deals are much cheaper than the alternative.

But despite the savings to be made, a great many people ignore them. Sometimes, they don’t even know the savings are on the table.

The way the system works sometimes actively works against us. Mobile phone contracts often include a new phone as part of the initial deal and they last for two years. A significant chunk of the monthly tariff over those two years is used to pay for the “free” handset that was given out at the outset.

But under the terms and conditions of almost all bill pay contracts, once the two years is up, you own the handset outright so obviously the monthly cost should fall.

Only it doesn’t.

After the first two years are up, a mobile provider can offer you a new phone in return for a new contract.

But if you’re happy with your current handset or don’t get the offer or contact your provider to arrange a better deal – the company will keep charging the original monthly fee.

Actually, they might even charge more because, over the two years, as a bill pay customer you will most likely have been hit with two automatically-imposed price hikes. Virgin Mobile is an exception to this rule.

So, if you sign up to a two-year contract with a monthly payment of €50 and continue to pay in full after the contract ends, you’re giving the company at least €40 a month for absolutely nothing. That is €480 a year.

According to admittedly self-interested research published by Sky Mobile to coincide with its arrival in the Irish mobile market a couple of years ago, about 300,000 people in Ireland are overpaying each year.

If they all overpay by €40 a month, then Ireland is collectively wasting close to €150 million every single year.

Under ComReg rules, the mobile phone providers “must make you aware that your contract is coming to an end and that you may cancel your current plan”.

“Your provider should also send you ‘best tariff advice’ highlighting the best tariff, price plan or bundle from your current service provider that suits your needs.”

No doubt that is done but if it is to make any difference you have to actually read the correspondence you are sent and we all know that is a big ask.

In a moderately ideal world, the price of your phone contract would automatically drop after two years to reflect what you are actually paying for, rather than what you were paying for at the start.

But our world is a long way from ideal, which is why you need to look after yourself.

If you own a phone outright the cheapest thing to do is to hang on to it and request your current provider to unlock the device, allowing you to switch to a SIM-only plan with another provider, or with the likes of Lidl.

The switching process is not overly complicated, although it is not always free of complications, and you obviously get to hang on to your existing number.

As well as Lidl and Tesco Mobile there is also the likes of Sky Mobile, Clear Mobile and GoMo, all of which piggyback on the main providers’ networks, so the level of coverage should be comparable.

That is not the only way to save.

A lot of higher-priced contracts are sold with the promise of huge amounts of data. But most users rarely exceed the standard amounts on the table, particularly if they are good at connecting to free wifi when out and about.

Another easy money-saving measure is a good haggle. Before your contract is due to end work out what the alternatives are and then demand better value. If you are getting nowhere with the person you are speaking to, ask to talk to someone in their retention unit; they might be more receptive to your threats to leave.

No matter who you are with or how much you are paying, do pay attention to roaming charges. Thankfully – because of our friends in Brussels – roaming charges are not the same money-grabbing gouging curse they once were (at least when you are using your phone across the EU) but if you are outside of the EU – or taking a ferry from Ireland to France, for instance – you could still be hit with a savagely high bill if you roam like you’re at home.

And do consider insurance. It can cost over €10 a month but if you are prone to breaking or losing your phone, it can be money well spent. Before you sign up, check if the contents insurance you have for your home covers personal possessions, as that might give you a safety net of sorts. If you do have specific mobile phone insurance and do change your handset, don’t assume the old policy will cover the new phone. It might not and that could see you paying for insurance on a phone you no longer have.

And if you are going SIM-only, consider buying second hand. There are a lot of platforms offering refurbished handsets for a whole lot less than they cost new, and even Apple sells refurbished phones. Just make sure you check the terms and conditions and make sure you have a degree of protection should things go wrong.

Business partners Graham Quinn and Sean Dooley are linked to Jessed Limited, the registered owner of the vacant number 21. The low-profile pair are also linked to a larger student accommodation group called Hazelwood Walk Holdings Limited, which owned €69 million of property at the end of 2025.

Brennans

Shoe shop Brennans is one of the oldest retailers in the area. Martin Brennan’s firm Blackbrook Limited still trades from number 11, which has been in family ownership since it was set up in 1881. It also owns number 10, according to recent planning records.

The Sherry family

Several Shop Street properties are linked to the Sherry family, who have controlled hospitality group Lydon House Catering since John Sherry led a management buyout in 1987. The company, which runs Donnelly’s of Barna, Franklin’s restaurant in Galway Shopping Centre and hospitality services for the Galway Races, has ties to the area going back decades to when Lydon’s restaurant traded from numbers 5 and 6. This premises is now owned by the family’s Minterburn Property Company. Land Registry and company records indicate that Minterburn also owns number 9 and has interests in parts of numbers 3-4 and 7-8. Its latest accounts record assets of €4 million.

McCambridges

McCambridges has been a staple of Shop Street for more than 100 years, and was kept in the family for three generations. In 2022, the supermarket at numbers 38 and 39 was sold to Musgrave Group for an undisclosed fee. Musgrave owns the property through subsidiary Cedarglade Limited.

Boots store

The family of the late Tim Naughton, who ran a hardware and furniture store from number 35, own the property now occupied by Boots. The property is held by Timon Securities Unlimited Company, which is owned by his wife Margaret Naughton and other family members. Naughton, who died in 2014, was a prominent Galway businessman, serving as chairman of The Connacht Tribune, Galway Bay FM and the Galway Race Committee.

Galway’s Taaffes shop, empty for 30 years, has a new owner

River Island store

The late Galway businessman Tom O’Connor ran O’Connors Audio Visual from Shop Street from 1970 to 1996 until it moved out of the city centre. The O’Connor family’s entity Hemoko Limited still owns its old premises at numbers 14 and 15, which are now occupied by River Island. The company, which lists his son Ronan as its sole director, valued its investment property at €6.5 million most recently. Land Registry records filed in 2022 showed another company led by O’Connor’s son Shane, called Roshin Limited, owns number 37, which houses shoe store Ecco. The property was valued at €1.7 million in its 2025 accounts.

Eason store

Asset manager MNK Partners has owned Eason’s store at number 33 since 2019, when it completed a €8.1 million sale-and-leaseback deal with the books retailer. The French firm, controlled by Mansour Khalife and Miranda Khabiri, has bought a number of Irish-based commercial property assets since it was formed in 2017. Eason’s store was recently put on the market by real estate agents Colliers for €7.5 million.

Number 34

The Divilly family’s connection to Shop Street began in the 1960s when Martin Divilly opened his butcher’s at number 34, but the store closed after being ravaged by a fire in 1979. Brian Divilly, who took over his father’s business in 1972, still owns the property that is vacant at ground level, but the upper floors are occupied by late bar Coyotes. The property is controlled by the businessman through Thornwood Property Holdings Limited, which valued its assets at €3.9 million at the end of 2025.

Three store

Number 1 is owned by the Lannon family, who control Mayo-based chicken producer Western Brand Group. They hold the property through Lannon Investments Limited, which is owned by Andrew, Clodagh, Seán and Eugene Lannon. The firm most recently valued its property at €2.6 million.

Lynch’s Castle

Lynch’s Castle at number 40, built around the 1500s, is now used by AIB as its main Galway city branch. Recent planning records show the property is still owned by AIB.

William Street

Garavan’s

Garavan’s bar has traded from William Street for almost 90 years, and its current proprietor Paul Garavan has retained a significant foothold in the area. Garavan owns numbers 42, 44, 46 and 48, from which jewellers Ór, Espresso 44, Rituals and his own pub trades. Filings show the properties are linked to Garavan’s firm MRCS Limited, which owned €17 million of investment property at the end of 2024.

Number 47

The building, which has been vacant for the past 30 years, was recently acquired by Tafko Limited, an entity linked to US-based investors Laura and Michael Higgins. The pair, both in their 60s, are behind several companies that own Galway properties, including Árd Rí House on Abbeygate Street Lower and the Bridge Mills building on Dominick Street Lower.

Mountain Warehouse store

Outdoor clothing store Mountain Warehouse relocated to numbers 31/33 in May from Mainguard Street. The store is owned by Patrick and Anne Jordan who are behind Atlantic Aviation Group and telecoms firm Secto Services, which reported combined turnover of €148 million and after-tax profits of €6.1 million in 2024.

Holland & Barrett store

Numbers 3 and 5, occupied by Holland & Barrett, are owned by Hill and Son (Galway) Unlimited Company, a firm led by directors Seamus and Michelle Hill. A recent planning application by Krispy Kreme relating to its William Street store stated Seamus Hill was also the owner of number 27.

A guide to who owns St Stephen’s Green, from wealthy Irish families to private clubs

Carrolls Irish Gifts and Galway Camera Shop stores

A number of companies linked to Mayo-based beef and lamb processor Martin Jennings Wholesale Limited have owned number 1 William Street and 10 and 12 Williamsgate Street since 2017. Three years ago, Land Registry filings named Killara Investments Unlimited Company as the buildings’ owner. It is controlled by businessman John Vaughan, who has been a shareholder in the aforementioned meat processing business for many years.

Fields the Jeweller store

In 2025, an update to Land Registry filings stated ET Burke Construction Limited was the owner of number 35, which is occupied by Fields the Jeweller. In April, owners of the firm Eamon and Marie Burke started a voluntary liquidation process.

Brown Thomas

Department store Brown Thomas, called Moon’s until the late 1990s, has an official address of 1-2 Eglinton Street, but fronts on to part of William Street. Brown Thomas Arnotts Limited, controlled by UK-based Selfridges Group, owns the property.

Williamsgate Street

The Colonial Buildings

The Colonial Buildings straddle the border of William Street and Williamsgate Street, but have an Eglinton Street address. Land Registry records show the property, built in 1866 and housing Beef and Lobster restaurant and Tomodachi sushi bar, is owned by Martin and Roisin Proulx’s Fides Playhouse Limited. The pair operate The Cellar Bar in the Colonial Buildings, Seven Bar and Restaurant nearby on Bridge Street and An File bar in Westport, Co Mayo. Their firm’s latest accounts showed it owned €11.5 million worth of property assets.

GBC Restaurant

The family-run GBC Restaurant has been operated from number 7 since 1936. The eatery, known for its traditional Irish breakfasts and carvery lunches, is run by Jeremiah and Brid McSweeney, who own the unit through GBC (Restaurant) Limited.

Hanley & Co

Men’s clothing store Hanley & Co, which was established in Galway in the 1960s by Joe Hanley, has traded in the city for more than 50 years. The business owns its store at number 8.

Fallers

Jeweller Stephen Faller opened his store on Williamsgate Street in 1899 and his family has traded from the Galway city centre location ever since. The family business, now run by managing director Paul Faller, owns its premises at number 10 and 12 through Stephen Faller (1879) Limited.

Eyre Square Centre

Located between numbers 9 and 10 Williamsgate Street is an entrance to Eyre Square Centre. The property, with 72 tenants, is owned by International Investment ICAV, which bought the centre in 2022. The ICAV is not required to disclose its underlying investors, so the beneficial investors are unknown. The centre is managed by David Goddard’s firm Lanthorn, which acquired Davy’s real estate business in 2024.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[The Irish Times Business Person of the Month: Donal Murphy, CEO DCC Energy]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/the-irish-times-business-person-of-the-month-donal-murphy-ceo-dcc-energy/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/the-irish-times-business-person-of-the-month-donal-murphy-ceo-dcc-energy/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 08:32:09 +0000DCC Energy chief executive Donal Murphy has been chosen as The Irish Times Business Person of the Month for September, an award run in association with Bank of Ireland.

During the month, Murphy, who has led the group since 2017, succeeded in securing shareholder approval for the Irish company’s sale to two US private equity firms in a deal worth up to £5.73 billion (€6.69 billion). This was in spite of opposition from some major shareholders, including the company’s founder Jim Flavin.

The deal, structured as a so-called scheme of arrangement, now requires High Court approval and is expected to complete in the first quarter of 2027.

“We’ve had a really strong turnout, and we’re very happy with the result,” Murphy said after the vote.

The buyers

DCC revealed in late April that it had received a €58-a-share offer from KKR and Energy Capital partners.

While the initial proposal was rejected, DCC agreed in late July to sell itself to the consortium for a £65.25-a-share upfront payment and the prospect of an additional payment related to the sale of its tech division.

The takeover deal valued the upfront cash offer at a 21.3 per cent premium to DCC’s closing share price in London on April 28th.

Once a conglomerate spanning various sectors, the Dublin-based but London-listed company is now focused on the energy sector.

Following the shareholder vote, Murphy signalled that he would like to remain on board to see out DCC’s goal to double the operating profit of the remaining energy division to £830 million between 2022 and 2030.

]]><![CDATA[Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/tech-sell-off-deepens-dents-rate-hike-bets/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/tech-sell-off-deepens-dents-rate-hike-bets/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 06:26:25 +0000Asian stocks extended losses, tracking declines on Wall Street as investors rotated out of technology giants following a blistering rally earlier this year and sought safety in US Treasuries and currencies such as the yen.

MSCI’s regional equities benchmark slipped 0.3 per cent, declining for a second day, leaving the gauge hovering around levels last seen in July.

Taiwan’s stock exchange will be shut Friday due to a typhoon. Sentiment stayed weak as contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.3 per cent in early Asian trading.

Earlier, the Nasdaq 100 tumbled 2.9 per cent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 6.7 per cent, their biggest declines since late June. Tesla and Meta Platforms were among the megacaps that came under pressure following their earnings. Instead of abandoning the stock market entirely, investors rotated into defensive dividend-paying staples and utilities.

Tech remained in focus as South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix scrapped an initial public offering for its US subsidiary Solidigm after facing shareholder opposition.

The rout in the artificial intelligence trade drove investors toward the safety of bonds, with Treasuries staging their biggest rally in more than two years. The benchmark 10-year yield declined 17 basis points to 4.95 per cent, while the yen outperformed all its major counterparts. Australian sovereign debt tracked the gains in Treasuries in early Asian trading.

Brent crude broadly held its gains to trade at around $113.10 per barrel. Oil rallied Thursday as deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over supplies.

Technology megacaps that powered a four-year bull run in US equities bore the brunt of the selling as earnings from megacap companies added to concerns their rebound since late March had gone too far, too quickly. The group faces fresh tests next week with results from Microsoft, Amazon.com. and Alphabet landing alongside the Federal Reserve’s policy decision.

“Sentiment seems to be shakier these days as investors reconsider AI-related assets,” said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank Ltd. “With US yields still elevated by recent standards, investors may want to hedge off some of these risks by seeking safety in Treasuries.”

Treasuries surged across the curve Thursday as the deepening rout in AI-related shares, turmoil in French markets and renewed Middle East tensions fueled haven buying. The rally pushed the 10-year yield below 5% for the first time in a month, with buying in Treasury futures accelerating as traders unwound bearish positions.

In other corners of the market, the yen extended its gains to 156.60 per dollar. The US currency was a touch weaker against most of its Group-of-10 peers.

Gold held its losses from Thursday’s session, when it slumped 2.8 per cent to trade just under $4,205 an ounce.

Concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment and its eventual payoff have knocked technology shares from recent highs and are beginning to weigh on the broader economic outlook. Traders also pared expectations for another Fed interest-rate increase this year.

Crude oil was another market that traders were paying attention to.

A drone strike on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah field killed two people without disrupting operations, while an attack on King Fahd International Airport caused casualties. Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on the Saudi port of Yanbu.

Investors are concerned that “post-election, the Iran war may escalate and potentially continue for a longer time than anticipated,” said Joseph Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading LLC. “The bond rally also confirms the risk-off approach.”

In Asia, Chinese stocks will be in focus after a $2.4 trillion slide from their May peak pushed them into a bear market. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. suffered its steepest drop in two months Thursday, dragging the Hang Seng Tech Index down 5%, its biggest decline since April 2025.

“Investor sentiment remains very poor for China’s onshore and offshore markets, and without new policy or tech catalysts, this kind of volatile, directionless environment may persist into early 2027,” said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore. - Bloomberg

   <title>In Königsmacherrolle und an Rand gedrängt</title>
   <description>Wenige Tage vor der Parlamentswahl in Israel am Dienstag ist völlig offen, wer künftig das Land regieren wird. Eine zentrale Rolle als Mehrheitsbeschaffer könnte den arabischen Parteien zufallen, insbesondere der islamisch-konservativen Ra’am-Partei von Mansur Abbas. Allerdings werden die arabischen Listen von den jüdischen Parteien an den Rand gedrängt und es wird offen Stimmung gegen eine Kooperation mit ihnen gemacht. Das hat wahltaktische Gründe – erst recht nach dem 7. Oktober.</description>

Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday.

Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term.

Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku!

Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi…

— Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday.

Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power.

However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them.

Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

How MPs from each parliamentary group voted on the bill (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all.

Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party.

“The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.”

“I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.”

 

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down.

However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen.

In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre).

Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk.

Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus.

They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026

On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”.

The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”.

Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority.

W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów.

Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby…

— Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026

The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues.

It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok.
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.
